text: Who first mentions this topic in the episode? Topic: {argument}
description: The topic may be worded differently from the transcript; the same subject under other words counts.

options.criteria: A host is the first speaker to name the topic or say something about it.
A non-host speaker is the first to name the topic or say something about it.
No speaker names the topic or says anything about it.

argument: a topic phrase taken from a line of this episode's transcript body, never from a host's opening lines (where the host previews the episode), or from a same-category episode and checked absent

text: Who first mentions this name in the episode? Name: {argument}
description: Misrecognised or misspelt forms of the same name count as the name. A pronoun alone does not.

options.criteria: A host is the first speaker to say the name.
A non-host speaker is the first to say the name.
No speaker says the name.

argument: a proper-noun phrase from a uniformly sampled line of this episode, not in a host's first line, or (one in three) from a same-category episode and checked absent

text: How many different speakers say this name in the episode? Name: {argument}
description: Misrecognised or misspelt forms of the same name count as the name. A pronoun alone does not.

options.criteria: No speaker says the name.
Exactly one speaker says the name, once or several times.
Two or more different speakers say the name.

argument: the same generator as ent-01, an independent draw

text: Which of these two names is said first in the episode? Names: {argument}
description: Misrecognised or misspelt forms of a name count as the name; a pronoun alone does not. If both are first said in the same line, answer for the one that comes first in that line.

options.criteria: Both names are said, and name A is said in an earlier line than name B.
Both names are said, and name B is said in an earlier line than name A.
Exactly one of the two names is said.
Neither name is said.

argument: two names from lines at least a quarter of the episode apart, neither containing a word of the other, rendered '(A) x; (B) y', A and B in random order

text: Who states an opinion on this topic? Topic: {argument}
description: An opinion is a sentence saying what the speaker thinks of the topic: that it is good or bad, right or wrong, or what they would want done about it. Facts, stories, questions, predictions and hopes are not opinions. Agreeing with another speaker counts only if the speaker restates the opinion in a sentence of their own.

options.criteria: At least one host states an opinion on the topic, and no non-host speaker does.
At least one non-host speaker states an opinion on the topic, and no host does.
At least one host and at least one non-host speaker state an opinion on the topic.
No speaker states an opinion on the topic, whether or not it is named.

argument: the episode's own description topic (`topic_own` in arguments.py: a noun phrase paraphrased from ep_description so it does not copy transcript wording)

text: Does a speaker say what happened to them because of this topic? Topic: {argument}
description: Feelings about the topic, hopes, and plans for the speaker's future are not things that happened.

options.criteria: At least one speaker tells, in a sentence, something that happened to them, their family or their work because of the topic.
The topic is named or talked about, and no speaker tells something that happened to them, their family or their work because of it.
No speaker names the topic or says anything about it.

argument: the same argument as top-03 (a transcript-body topic)

text: How many different speakers talk about this topic? Topic: {argument}
description: A speaker counts only through a line of four or more words about the topic; a single word of agreement does not count.

options.criteria: No speaker names the topic or says anything about it.
Exactly one speaker says something about the topic, once or several times.
Two or more different speakers say something about the topic.

argument: the episode's own description topic (`topic_own`, as top-04)

text: Does a speaker give listeners advice about this topic? Topic: {argument}
description: Advice is a speaker telling listeners to do or avoid something in their own lives; 'you' and 'people' address listeners, advice to another speaker alone does not count.

options.criteria: A speaker tells listeners to do or avoid an action that is the topic or a named part of it.
The topic is named or talked about, and no speaker tells listeners to do or avoid anything about it.
No speaker names the topic or says anything about it.

text: Does a speaker say who or what this name is? Name: {argument}
description: Misrecognised or misspelt forms of the same name count as the name. The explanation may come in a different line from the name, before or after it.

options.criteria: A speaker states in words what kind of person, place, organisation or thing the name is, or how it relates to a speaker, in a clause whose subject is the name or a pronoun for it.
The name is said, and no speaker states who or what it is; a meaning clear only from context does not count.
No speaker says the name.

argument: the same argument as ent-01 (a different question on the same name)

text: Is this name said in a question that a speaker asks? Name: {argument}
description: Misrecognised or misspelt forms of the same name count as the name; a pronoun alone does not, and a name of two or more words counts only when all its words are said together ('Stoll' alone is not 'Clifford Stoll'). A question is a sentence phrased as a direct question ('is it', 'did you', 'what about X'), rhetorical ones included, or any sentence ending in a question mark. Where a line ends before its sentence does, the words at the start of the next line up to the first full stop or question mark belong to that sentence, whoever that line is labelled as, so a question mark at the start of the next line ends the sentence before it. A statement with a tag at the end ('right?', 'you know?') is a statement. Indirect questions and requests without a question mark ('I wonder whether X', 'tell us about X') are statements. A question quoted from someone who is not a speaker in this episode is a statement.

options.criteria: At least one sentence that says the name is a question a speaker asks in the conversation, whoever asks it and whether or not it is answered.
The name is said, and no sentence that says it is a question a speaker asks in the conversation.
No speaker says the name.

text: Does any one speaker say both of these names? Names: {argument}
description: Misrecognised or misspelt forms of a name count as the name; a pronoun alone does not. A name of two or more words counts only when all its words are said together; a part said alone ('Stoll' for 'Clifford Stoll') does not count. Every word in a line belongs to that line's speaker label, and labels are taken as written: host_1 and host_2 are different speakers, and so are two labels that seem to be one person. A name said in an advert or a played clip belongs to the label on that line. The order of A and B does not matter.

options.criteria: Both names are said, and the lines of at least one speaker label say both names.
Both names are said, and no single speaker label's lines say both names.
Exactly one of the two names is said.
Neither name is said.

argument: the same argument as ord-02 (`name_pair`), rendered '(A) x; (B) y'

text: Is this topic talked about again after the conversation has moved away from it? Topic: {argument}
description: The topic may be worded differently from the transcript; the same subject under other words counts. A bare naming of the topic in a list, an opening preview or a closing recap is not saying something about it. Lines of fewer than four words, and lines that carry on the same discussion only through a pronoun ("it", "that", "this", "he", "she", "they"), are skipped when counting the lines between: they neither separate nor join, and a line of fewer than four words is not a mention either.

options.criteria: A speaker says something about the topic, then three or more consecutive lines of four or more words are not about it, and then a speaker says something about the topic again.
The topic is named or talked about, and no two lines that say something about it are separated by three or more consecutive lines of four or more words that are not about it.
No speaker names the topic or says anything about it.

argument: the same argument as top-03 (`topic_body`, a phrase from the middle window or planted absent)

text: Does a speaker give a specific number as a fact about this topic? Topic: {argument}
description: The topic may be worded differently from the transcript; the number must be in the same sentence as the topic's subject or a synonym for it, not merely in the same line. A specific number is a count, amount of money, percentage, score or measurement stated as a fact; approximate figures ('about 30 million') count, vague quantities ('a lot', 'hundreds of') do not. Dates, years, durations, ages, times of day, episode numbers, positions in a ranking or order ('the 25th pick'), ratings given as opinions ('an eight out of ten'), phone numbers and addresses do not count, and neither do numbers in adverts or sponsor reads, in questions, or in imagined or hypothetical examples.

options.criteria: At least one sentence that names the topic's own subject or a synonym for it gives a specific number as a fact about that subject.
The topic is named or talked about, and no sentence that names its subject or a synonym for it gives a specific number as a fact about that subject.
No speaker names the topic or says anything about it.

argument: the episode's own description topic (`topic_own`, as top-04)

text: Does a speaker predict what will happen to this topic? Topic: {argument}
description: The topic may be worded differently from the transcript. A prediction is a statement about a future event outside the speaker's own control; hedged ones ('I think it will', 'probably') count. Saying only that something might or could happen, hopes, wishes, plans for the speakers' own actions, questions about the future, 'if' statements about what would happen under a condition, and predictions the speaker reports from someone else without saying they agree do not count.

options.criteria: In a sentence that names the topic's own subject or a synonym for it, a speaker states that something about that subject will or will not happen, or will change, in the future.
The topic is named or talked about, and no sentence that names its subject or a synonym for it predicts what will happen to that subject.
No speaker names the topic or says anything about it.

argument: the episode's own description topic (`topic_own`, as top-04)
